chunks: Ja'far ibn Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abdullah ibn al-Mughira al-Kufi (may God be pleased with him) narrated that his grandfather al-Hasan ibn Ali narrated to him, from his great-grandfather Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father (peace be upon them both)

He said: Seven groups of people do not shorten their prayer: the tax collector who travels for his collection; the commander who travels for his governance; the merchant who travels in his trade from market to market; the shepherd; the Bedouin who seeks places of water and growth of plants; the man who seeks game, desiring it for the amusement of this world; and the warrior who cuts off the path (bandit).
ai.seo_question: Who are the seven groups exempt from shortening prayers while traveling?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq highlights these seven categories to illustrate the juristic principle that 'mobility of purpose' rather than mere physical distance determines the status of a traveler (musafir). This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on practical ease (rukhas), ensuring that those whose livelihoods depend on constant movement are not burdened by the stricter requirements of full prayer (tamam).
